title: Blocking queue (producer-consumer)
points: Coordination is about how threads communicate and hand work off to each other, as opposed to protecting shared state.
A blocking queue is a thread-safe queue where producers put work in and consumers take it out.
put() blocks when a bounded queue is full and take() blocks when it is empty, so the queue handles waiting for you without wait/notify.
It solves the producer-consumer problem and gives back-pressure: a fast producer is slowed down when consumers can't keep up.

When a producer adds to a full bounded queue there are three choices: put(e) blocks until space frees up, offer(e) returns false immediately, and offer(e, timeout, unit) waits up to the timeout and then returns false.
trade: Use it when one side generates work and another processes it at a different speed (request handlers and a worker pool, log writer, job queue). Prefer a bounded queue so memory can't grow without limit. Versus an actor: a blocking queue is a shared queue that many consumers pull from, while an actor owns private state behind its own single mailbox. Versus locks: you hand the data over instead of sharing it. Choosing the put variant: put() when the producer should simply slow down (back-pressure) and can safely wait; offer(e) when it must never block and can drop, retry later or reject the request (load shedding); offer with timeout when it can wait a bounded time, then fail or fall back so a stuck consumer can't hang the producer forever. Consumers have the same trio: take(), poll(), poll(timeout, unit).
test: A fast API thread produces report jobs and a slow worker generates them. Without limits memory grows until the app crashes. What do you use, and when would you pick put(), offer() or offer with a timeout?
answer: A bounded blocking queue. put() blocks the producer (back-pressure) when full, offer() returns false at once so you can reject or drop, and offer with a timeout waits a bounded time then returns false.

questions.question: What happens when a producer calls put() on a full bounded blocking queue?
options: It blocks until a consumer makes space
questions.explanation: put() waits, which is how back-pressure works. Dropping or growing are separate policies (offer, unbounded queues).

questions.question: Which problem does a blocking queue solve most directly?
options: Producer-consumer hand-off between threads running at different speeds
Many players each holding private state
questions.explanation: It coordinates hand-off and waiting. A counter wants an atomic, and per-entity private state suits actors.

questions.question: Why prefer a bounded queue over an unbounded one?
options: It limits memory and slows producers when consumers lag
questions.explanation: Unbounded queues hide overload until memory runs out. A bound turns overload into back-pressure.

questions.question: A request thread adds jobs to a full bounded queue and must respond quickly, returning 503 if the system is overloaded. Which call fits?
options: put(job), blocking until there is space
offer(job), returning false immediately so it can reject the request
Replace the queue with an unbounded one
questions.explanation: offer() never blocks, so the caller can shed load at once. put() could hang the request thread while consumers are slow.

questions.question: How does offer(e, 2, SECONDS) differ from put(e) on a full queue?
options: It waits at most 2 seconds and then returns false instead of waiting indefinitely
It grows the queue after 2 seconds
questions.explanation: The timeout bounds the wait, so a stalled consumer cannot block the producer forever. put() has no bound; offer(e) has zero wait.
